entry.title: A new bound on the size of the largest critical set in a Latin square
entry.summary: A critical set in an n x n array is a set C of given entries, such that there exists a unique extension of C to an n x n Latin square and no proper subset of C has this property. The cardinality of the largest critical set in any Latin square of order n is denoted by lcs(n). In 1978 Curran and van Rees proved that lcs(n) <= n^2 - n. Here we show that lcs(n) <= n^2-3n+3.

entry.title: A lower bound for the size of the largest critical sets in Latin squares
entry.summary: A critical set in an $n \times n$ array is a set $C$ of given entries, such that there exists a unique extension of $C$ to an $n\times n$ Latin square and no proper subset of $C$ has this property. The cardinality of the largest critical set in any Latin square of order $n$ is denoted by $\lcs{n}$. We give a lower bound for $\lcs{n}$ by showing that $\lcs{n} \geq n^2(1-\frac{2 + \ln 2}{\ln n})+n(1+\frac {\ln (8 π)} {\ln n})-\frac{\ln 2}{\ln n}.$
entry.arxiv:journal_ref: Bulletin of the Institute of Combinatorics and its Applications (Canada). 38 (2003) pp.19-22

entry.title: On the size of the minimum critical set of a Latin square
entry.summary: A critical set in an $n \times n$ array is a set $C$ of given entries, such that there exists a unique extension of $C$ to an $n\times n$ Latin square and no proper subset of $C$ has this property. For a Latin square $L$, $\scs{L}$ denotes the size of the smallest critical set of $L$, and $\scs{n}$ is the minimum of $\scs{L}$ over all Latin squares $L$ of order $n$. We find an upper bound for the number of partial Latin squares of size $k$ and prove that $$n^2-(e+o(1))n^{10/6} \le \max \scs{L} \le n^2-\frac{\sqrtπ}{2}n^{9/6}.$$ % This improves a result of N. Cavenagh (Ph.D. thesis, The University of Queensland, 2003) and disproves one of his conjectures. Also it improves the previously known lower bound for the size of the largest critical set of any Latin square of order $n$.

entry.title: Critical Sets in Latin Squares and Associated Structures
entry.summary: A critical set in a Latin square of order $n$ is a set of entries in an $n\times n$ array which can be embedded in precisely one Latin square of order $n$, with the property that if any entry of the critical set is deleted, the remaining set can be embedded in more than one Latin square of order $n$. The cardinality of the largest critical set in any Latin square of order $n$ is denoted by $lcs(n)$. In 1978 Curran and van Rees proved that $lcs(n)\leq n^2-n$. In Chapter 4, it is shown that $lcs(n)\leq n^2-3n+3$. Chapter 5 provides new bounds on the maximum number of intercalates in Latin squares of orders $2^αm$ and $2^αm+1$, and a new lower bound on $lcs(4m)$. In Chapter 6 a construction is given which verifies the existence of a critical set of size $\displaystyle{\frac{n^2}{4}} + 1$ when $n$ is even and $n\geq 6$. In Chapter 7 the representation of Steiner trades of volume less than or equal to nine is examined. Computational results are used to identify those trades for which the associated partial Latin square can be decomposed into six disjoint Latin interchanges. Chapter 8 focusses on critical sets in Latin squares of order at most six and extensive computational routines are used to identify all the critical sets of different sizes in these Latin squares.
entry.arxiv:comment: PhD thesis, The University of Queensland, April 2001 (degree approved November 2001). 133 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Thesis abstract published in Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. 66(1) (2002) 175-176. Material from Chapter 4 also appeared in arXiv:math/0107159
